## Problem

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $x_0\in\Omega$.

Define the Dirac delta at $x_0$ by

$$
\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)
=
\varphi(x_0),
\qquad
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).
$$

Prove that $\delta_{x_0}$ is a distribution on $\Omega$.

## Solution

Recall that a distribution on $\Omega$ is a continuous linear functional on the space of test functions

$$
\mathcal D(\Omega)
=
C_c^\infty(\Omega).
$$

Thus we need to prove that

$$
\delta_{x_0}:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb R
$$

is linear and continuous.

### Linearity

Let $\varphi,\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{x_0}(a\varphi+b\psi)
&=
(a\varphi+b\psi)(x_0)\\
&=
a\varphi(x_0)+b\psi(x_0)\\
&=
a\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)
+
b\delta_{x_0}(\psi).
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $\delta_{x_0}$ is linear.

### Continuity

Let $K\subset\Omega$ be compact. For every

$$
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)
$$

with

$$
\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset K,
$$

we have

$$
|\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)|
=
|\varphi(x_0)|.
$$

If $x_0\notin K$, then

$$
\varphi(x_0)=0,
$$

and hence

$$
\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)=0.
$$

If $x_0\in K$, then

$$
|\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)|
=
|\varphi(x_0)|
\leq
\sup_{x\in K}|\varphi(x)|.
$$

Therefore, in either case,

$$
|\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)|
\leq
\sup_{x\in K}|\varphi(x)|.
$$

The right-hand side is one of the standard seminorms defining the topology of

$$
C_c^\infty(\Omega).
$$

Hence $\delta_{x_0}$ is continuous.

Equivalently, suppose that

$$
\varphi_j\to0
\quad\text{in }\mathcal D(\Omega).
$$

Then there exists a compact set

$$
K\subset\Omega
$$

such that

$$
\operatorname{supp}\varphi_j\subset K
$$

for all sufficiently large $j$, and

$$
\sup_{x\in K}
|D^\alpha\varphi_j(x)|
\to0
$$

for every multi-index $\alpha$.

Taking $\alpha=0$, we obtain

$$
\sup_{x\in K}|\varphi_j(x)|
\to0.
$$

Hence

$$
|\delta_{x_0}(\varphi_j)|
=
|\varphi_j(x_0)|
\leq
\sup_{x\in K}|\varphi_j(x)|
\to0.
$$

Therefore $\delta_{x_0}$ is continuous on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$.

We conclude that

$$
\boxed{
\delta_{x_0}\in\mathcal D'(\Omega).
}
$$

Thus the Dirac delta is a distribution.

## Remark

The Dirac delta is a distribution of order zero, since

$$
|\delta_{x_0}(\varphi)|
\leq
\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}.
$$

It is not induced by any locally integrable function.

Indeed, if there were some

$$
f\in L_{\mathrm{loc}}^1(\Omega)
$$

such that

$$
\varphi(x_0)
=
\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx
$$

for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, then testing against functions supported away from $x_0$ would imply

$$
f=0
$$

almost everywhere on

$$
\Omega\setminus\{x_0\}.
$$

Since the singleton $\{x_0\}$ has Lebesgue measure zero, this would imply

$$
f=0
$$

almost everywhere in $\Omega$, contradicting

$$
\delta_{x_0}\neq0.
$$

Thus the Dirac delta is a genuine distribution rather than an ordinary function.
